notes.meaning: God brought another enemy against Solomon named Rezon from the kingdom of Zobah to the north. Rezon had run away from his own master, King Hadadezer, when King David defeated the army of Zobah years earlier. Even when enemies act out of personal hatred or ambition, God can use them to bring needed discipline to his people.

After the defeat of Zobah, Rezon gathered a band of raiders and became their leader. They lived as outlaws until they managed to seize the key city of Damascus, where Rezon established himself as king. This took place as Israel's border defenses weakened in the later years of Solomon.

Rezon remained a bitter rival of Israel during the rest of Solomon's reign, ruling over the region of Aram from Damascus. Together with Hadad from Edom in the south, Rezon troubled Israel from the north. Solomon had known great peace when he followed God, but his turn to idols brought unrest on both borders.

Now the story turns to an enemy from within Israel itself, a man named Jeroboam son of Nebat from the tribe of Ephraim. He was raised by a widowed mother named Zeruah and worked in the service of Solomon. In time, Jeroboam turned against the king and attempted a rebellion.

This explains the setting that led to Jeroboam's rise and rebellion. Solomon was carrying out massive building projects, including filling in the terraces called the Millo and closing gaps in the defensive walls of Jerusalem. These heavy construction tasks required large crews of workers and opened the door for complaints about forced labor.

Jeroboam was a capable, energetic, and courageous young man. When Solomon noticed how hard he worked, he promoted him to supervise the forced laborers from Ephraim and Manasseh, known as the house of Joseph. This position gave Jeroboam great influence and put him in close contact with the restless northern tribes.

One day, as Jeroboam was walking out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah from Shiloh met him on the road. Ahijah was wearing a brand-new cloak, and the two men were alone out in the open country. God arranged this quiet meeting so the prophet could deliver a private message directly to Jeroboam.

Ahijah grabbed his new cloak and ripped it into twelve separate pieces. Biblical prophets often acted out a message with real objects to make God's word vivid and unforgettable. The twelve pieces stood for the twelve tribes of Israel, showing that the whole nation was about to be torn apart.

Ahijah told Jeroboam to take ten of the torn pieces for himself. The Lord declared that he was tearing the kingdom away from Solomon's family and giving ten of the tribes to Jeroboam to rule. This was the first clear warning that the unified nation of Israel would soon divide into two separate kingdoms.

God made clear that one tribe would remain under David's royal family for the sake of David and Jerusalem. Benjamin was closely tied to Judah, and together they formed this single southern territory centered around the holy city. God preserved this portion to keep his ancient promise to David and to honor the place he chose for his temple.

The Lord explained why this judgment had to fall: Solomon and many Israelites had turned away from the Lord to worship false gods, including Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom. They abandoned God's laws and refused to follow him with loyal hearts the way King David had done. Turning to idols always shatters the peace and unity of God's people.

Even so, God would not strip the kingdom away from Solomon during his own lifetime. Solomon would remain the ruler for all his days, not because he earned it, but because of God's covenant with his father David, who had faithfully obeyed God's commands. God's faithfulness outlasts human failure.

The division would wait until the next generation, when God would take the ten northern tribes from Solomon's son and hand them over to Jeroboam. This showed that God was patient, yet completely sure to carry out his word. Jeroboam was warned by this timing not to try to seize the throne before God gave it to him.

Solomon's son would keep one tribe so that David would always have a lamp burning before the Lord in Jerusalem. A lamp represents a living heir whose royal line does not go out, ensuring that the throne continues to shine with God's presence. Christians see this promise ultimately fulfilled in Jesus, the great descendant of David who rules forever.

The Lord promised to raise up Jeroboam and give him everything his heart had secretly desired by making him king over the northern tribes of Israel. Jeroboam had been ambitious for power, and God was now offering to fulfill that hope in his own sovereign time. True authority comes only from God's hand, not from human scheming.

God offered Jeroboam an amazing promise: if he walked in obedience and kept God's commands as David did, God would establish an enduring family dynasty for him in Israel just like the one built for David. The future of Jeroboam's house hung completely on his loyalty to the Lord. Tragically, Jeroboam would later walk away from God and lose this great promise.

God stated that he would humble David's descendants because of Solomon's idolatry, but the discipline would not last forever. The royal line would suffer heavy losses, yet God would never completely cast it away. In time, the promised Messiah would come from David's family to bring everlasting restoration and peace to God's people.

When Solomon learned about what was happening, he tried to put Jeroboam to death to protect his own crown. Jeroboam escaped to Egypt and found protection under King Shishak, staying there until Solomon died. It was foolish for Solomon to try to stop what God had already decreed, just as it was foolish for Jeroboam to rush ahead instead of waiting patiently on the Lord.

The writer notes that the rest of what Solomon did, along with the details of his great wisdom, were recorded in an official record called the Book of the Acts of Solomon. This court record, which included writings by royal prophets, is now lost to history. The Bible selects the parts of history that teach us about God's covenant and his ways.

Solomon ruled in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years. His reign lasted as long as his father David's, but his life was cut relatively short, likely dying around age sixty. God had promised Solomon long life if he stayed faithful, but wandering into sin brought an early end to his days.

Solomon died, rested with his ancestors, and was buried in the city of David his father. His son Rehoboam then took the throne in his place. The golden age of Israel's united kingdom came to a close with dark clouds gathering over its future.

differ.view: Solomon truly repented of his sins before he died and was saved, as seen in his writing of Ecclesiastes and God's covenant promise that his mercy would never be fully taken from him.
Scripture deliberately leaves Solomon's repentance uncertain so that believers will take warning and not presume on God's mercy when they fall into sin.
The phrase about resting with his fathers simply means Solomon died, and because the text records no turning back to God, we cannot say with confidence that he was saved.
